{{Short description|Graph representing connectivity between cliques of another graph}}
[[File:Simplex graph.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|A graph {{mvar|G}} and the corresponding simplex graph {{math|κ(''G'')}}. The blue-colored node in {{math|κ(''G'')}} corresponds to the zero-vertex clique in {{mvar|G}} (the empty set), and the magenta node corresponds to the 3-vertex clique.]]

In [[graph theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''simplex graph''' {{math|κ(''G'')}} of an [[undirected graph]] {{mvar|G}} is itself a graph, with one [[Vertex (graph theory)|node]] for each [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] (a set of mutually adjacent vertices) in {{mvar|G}}. Two nodes of {{math|κ(''G'')}} are linked by an edge whenever the corresponding two cliques differ in the presence or absence of a single vertex.

The empty set is included as one of the cliques of {{mvar|G}} that are used to form the clique graph, as is every set of one vertex and every set of two adjacent vertices. Therefore, the simplex graph contains within it a [[subdivision (graph theory)|subdivision]] of {{mvar|G}} itself. The simplex graph of a [[complete graph]] is a [[hypercube graph]], and the simplex graph of a [[cycle graph]] of length four or more is a [[gear graph]]. The simplex graph of the [[complement graph]] of a [[path graph]] is a [[Fibonacci cube]].

The complete subgraphs of {{mvar|G}} can be given the structure of a [[median algebra]]: the median of three cliques {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}} is formed by the vertices that belong to a [[Majority function|majority]] of the three cliques.<ref>{{harvtxt|Barthélemy|Leclerc|Monjardet|1986}}, page 200.</ref> Any two vertices belonging to this median set must both belong to at least one of {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, or {{mvar|C}}, and therefore must be linked by an edge, so the median of three cliques is itself a clique. The simplex graph is the [[median graph]] corresponding to this median algebra structure. When {{mvar|G}} is the [[complement graph]] of a [[bipartite graph]], the cliques of {{mvar|G}} can be given a stronger structure as a [[distributive lattice]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Propp|1997}}.</ref> and in this case the simplex graph is the graph of the lattice. As is true for median graphs more generally, every simplex graph is itself [[bipartite graph|bipartite]].

The simplex graph has one vertex for every simplex in the [[clique complex]] {{math|''X''(''G'')}} of {{mvar|G}}, and two vertices are linked by an edge when one of the two corresponding simplexes is a facet of the other. Thus, the objects (vertices in the simplex graph, simplexes in {{math|''X''(''G'')}}) and relations between objects (edges in the simplex graph, inclusion relations between simplexes in {{math|''X''(''G'')}}) are in one-to-one correspondence between {{math|''X''(''G'')}} and {{math|κ(''G'')}}.

Simplex graphs were introduced by {{harvtxt|Bandelt|van de Vel|1989}},<ref>{{harvtxt|Imrich|Klavžar|Mulder|1999}} credit the introduction of simplex graphs to a later paper, also by Bandelt and van de Vel, but this appears to be a mistake.</ref> who observed that a simplex graph has no cubes if and only if the underlying graph is [[triangle-free graph|triangle-free]], and showed that the [[chromatic number]] of the underlying graph equals the minimum number {{mvar|n}} such that the simplex graph can be isometrically embedded into a [[Cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian product]] of {{mvar|n}} trees. As a consequence of the existence of [[Mycielskian|triangle-free graphs with high chromatic number]], they showed that there exist two-dimensional topological [[median algebra]]s that cannot be embedded into products of finitely many [[real tree]]s. {{harvtxt|Imrich|Klavžar|Mulder|1999}} also use simplex graphs as part of their proof that testing whether a graph is triangle-free or whether it is a median graph may be performed equally quickly.
